summary: Specifies a new type, the Key ID Information Type, for the General Extension Payload of the Multimedia Internet KEYing protocol. It is used, for example, in the 3GPP Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: MIKEY is the protocol that hands out encryption keys for multimedia sessions. This RFC adds a small extra part to a MIKEY message that says which kind of key it carries and which key it is, so a receiver can tell a group key from a traffic key even when several travel together.

questions: what is the mikey key id type
what is the mikey general extension payload
what is the mikey empty map type
subtitle: Telling receivers which kind of key a MIKEY message carries, and which key it is.

tldr.problem: MIKEY messages carry keys, but the protocol had no way to say what kind of key a given message holds or which key it refers to.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Key ID Information payload type, number 3, to the MIKEY General Extension payload, made of Key ID Type sub-payloads that name the kind of key and carry its identifier, together with an empty-map value for the crypto session ID map type.
tldr.outcome: MIKEY can now carry several different kinds of key in one message and identify each of them, which is what MBMS key re-keying needs, and the new values were registered with IANA.

facts.label: Empty map CS ID map type

today: RFC 4563 is a Proposed Standard and the IANA registries it created were later extended by RFC 6309, which sets out the IANA rules for MIKEY. The payload type 3 and the Key ID types 0 to 2 remain the registered values for naming the keys carried in a MIKEY message.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) is involved in the development of a multicast and broadcast service, the Multimedia Broadcast/Multicast Service (MBMS), and its security architecture. MBMS requires the use of the Multimedia Internet KEYing protocol to convey the keys and related security parameters needed to secure multimedia that is multicast or broadcast.

One of the requirements MBMS puts on security is the ability to perform frequent updates of the keys. The rationale is that it will be costly for subscribers to redistribute the decryption keys to non-subscribers, and the cost of redistributing the keys using the unicast channel should be higher than the cost of purchasing the keys for this scheme to have an effect. To implement this, MBMS uses a three-level key management to distribute group keys to the clients and to be able to re-key by pushing down a new group key. MBMS therefore needs to identify which types of keys are involved in the MIKEY message and their identity.

This memo specifies a new type for the General Extension payload in MIKEY, to identify the type and identity of keys involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadcast services change their keys often, because handing a new key to every subscriber by unicast message would be far too expensive. To re-key often, a receiver has to be told which of several keys a message is about.

sections.title: The Three-Level Key Management of MBMS
sections.content:
An application where this extension is used is MBMS key management, which uses three levels of keys. Clients refers to the clients who have subscribed to a given multicast or broadcast service.

  • The MBMS User Key (MUK) is a point-to-point key between the multicast server and each client.
  • The MBMS Service Key (MSK) is a group key between the multicast server and all the clients.
  • The MBMS Traffic Key (MTK) is a group traffic key between the multicast server and all clients.

The Traffic Keys are the keys that are regularly updated. The point-to-point MUK is shared between the multicast server and the client, and is used as a pre-shared key to run MIKEY with the pre-shared key method and to deliver the MSK point-to-point. The same MSK is pushed to all the clients to be used as a second-level group key. The MSK is then used to push to all the clients an MTK, the third-level key, which is the actual group key used for the protection of the media traffic. For example, the MTK could be the master key for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol in the streaming case.

A Key Domain identifier defines the domain where the group keys are valid or applicable, for example a specific service provider. To allow the key distribution described above, an indication of the type and identity of the keys being carried in a MIKEY message is needed, and this indication is carried in the new Type of the General Extension payload.
sections.plainLanguage: MBMS nests its keys. A per-subscriber key unlocks a service key shared by everyone, and the service key unlocks the traffic key that actually protects the media. Only the traffic key changes often, and each level has to be named in the message that carries it.

sections.title: How the Extension Fits MIKEY
sections.content:
According to RFC 3830, MIKEY is a registration protocol that supports re-keying for unicast in the terms of the MSEC Group Key Management Architecture. MBMS uses MIKEY both as a registration protocol and as a re-key protocol, and the specified extension implements the necessary additions to RFC 3830 that allow MIKEY to function both as a unicast and multicast re-key protocol in the MBMS setting.

It is also necessary to specify what Crypto Session ID map type is associated with a given key. There are cases, for example the download case in MBMS, where the required parameters are signalled in-band, each downloaded Digital Rights Management Content Format object containing the parameters needed by the receiver to process it. Since those parameters are not transported by MIKEY, a Crypto Session ID map type needs to be registered to the empty map, to be used when the map and policy information are conveyed outside of MIKEY.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY was designed for one-to-one sessions. Using it for a broadcast means adding the missing pieces: the ability to name the kind of key, and a way to say that the session mapping is not carried in this message at all.

sections.title: The Key ID Information Payload
sections.content:
The General Extension payload in MIKEY is defined in section 6.15 of RFC 3830. The General Extension payload type defined here, the Key ID Information, is not restricted to MBMS. Applications using this General Extension payload type may define new Key ID types, and these applications must define the semantics and usage of the Key ID Type sub-payloads according to section 8 of this document. The MBMS use of the Key ID Type sub-payloads is specified in the 3GPP specification.

The Key ID Information Type, number 3, formats the General Extension payload with a Next Payload field, a Type field and a Length field, followed by the Key ID Information field, which is the general payload data transporting the type and identifier of a key and is formed by Key ID Type sub-payloads. Next Payload and Length are defined in section 6.15 of RFC 3830. The Type field is 8 bits and identifies the type of the General Extension payload; this memo adds Type 3 to the ones already defined in RFC 3830.

The Key ID Type sub-payload carries a Key ID Type field of 8 bits that describes the type of the key ID, a Key ID Length field of 8 bits that describes the length of the Key ID field in octets, and a Key ID field of variable length that defines the identity of the key. The predefined Key ID types are 0 for the MBMS Key Domain ID, the ID of the group key domain; 1 for the MBMS Service Key ID, the ID of the group key; and 2 for the MBMS Traffic Key ID, the ID of the group traffic key.

There may be more than one Key ID Type sub-payload in an extension, and the overall length, the sum of the lengths of all Key ID Type sub-payloads, of the Key ID information field cannot exceed 2^16 - 1 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The new payload holds a list of small sub-payloads. Each one says which kind of key it is talking about and then carries that key's identifier. Several can appear in one message, and the whole list must stay under 65535 octets.

sections.title: The Empty Map CS ID Map Type
sections.content:
When the security policy information is conveyed outside of MIKEY, the Crypto Session ID map type is set to the value defined for the empty map, which is 1. In this case there must not be any Security Policy payload present in the message.

This value exists because the map and policy information is sometimes delivered in band, as part of the protected content itself, and in that case the MIKEY message has nothing to map. The empty map says exactly that, so that a receiver does not go looking for a policy that was never sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the rules for a session travel inside the content rather than inside the key message. The empty map value records that, so nobody waits for a security policy that is not coming.

sections.title: Transport Considerations
sections.content: As specified in section 7 of RFC 3830, the underlying transport of the MIKEY protocol has to be defined for each type of transport. When the Key ID payload is used with MBMS, the transport is UDP, and the usage of MIKEY over UDP in the MBMS setting is defined in the 3GPP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY needs a transport named for each kind of network. For the broadcast service the transport is UDP, and the 3GPP specification says how it is used there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The usage of MIKEY for updating the traffic encryption key in the broadcast manner deviates from the way MIKEY was originally designed. Two main points relate to the security of the described usage.

First, the delivery of the traffic key is not source origin authenticated, but is protected by a group MAC keyed by the service key. The threat this raises is that users who are part of the group can send fake traffic key messages to other group members. The origin of the traffic key messages is a node inside the core network, and the trust model used in MBMS is that only trusted traffic is allowed to be sent, from within the operator's network, on the MBMS bearers. There is always the risk that traffic is injected on the air interface between the base stations and the user equipment, so it is possible for members of the group to spoof traffic key updates to other members. 3GPP decided that the technical difficulties and costs involved in performing such an attack are large enough compared to the expected gain for the attacker that the risk was deemed acceptable. Since the delivery of the traffic key is not source origin authenticated, there is nothing gained by adding source origin authentication to the RTP streams, for example using SRTP-TESLA, and the use of the specified extension is therefore not compatible with SRTP-TESLA, which requires source origin authentication of the integrity key. In MBMS the service key is protected end-to-end from the multicast server to the clients using the client-unique MUK, but the traffic key is delivered under protection by the service key, so source origin authentication is not achieved.

Second, the delivery of the traffic key is separated from the delivery of the security policy. The security policy is delivered with the service key. The delivery of the traffic keys is assumed to be frequent, and some scenarios require it to be as frequent as a few seconds apart, which would make the bandwidth cost very high if the security policy were delivered together with each traffic key. The security policy parameters of the streaming session are not anticipated to change during the session, even though the traffic key is updated, so 3GPP decided there was no need for updating the policy during an ongoing session. Updating the policy during an ongoing session would still be possible by updating the service key.

The empty map type used when the security policy is delivered in band relies on the security provided by the Digital Rights Management Content Format, and MIKEY is in that case only used to provide the master key for the content processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are weaker than in ordinary MIKEY. The traffic key is protected by the shared service key, so anyone who has that key could try to send a fake update, and 3GPP judged the cost of that attack high enough to accept the risk. The rules for the session travel with the service key rather than with each traffic key update, because they rarely change.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
According to section 10 of RFC 3830, IETF consensus is required to register values in the range 0-240 in the Type namespace of the MIKEY General Extension payload and in the CS ID map type namespace of the Common Header payload.

A new value in the MIKEY General Extension payload Type namespace has been registered, and the registered value for Key ID is 3. The value 1 has also been registered for the empty map in the existing CS ID map namespace of the Common Header payload.

A new namespace for the Key ID Type field has been established and will be managed by IANA. The IANA has registered the predefined types of the Key ID table, and will also manage the definition of additional values in the future. Values in the range 0-240 for each namespace should be approved by the process of IETF consensus, and values in the range 241-255 are reserved for Private Use, according to RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA now keeps three new lists: the payload types, the key identifier types and the empty map value. Ordinary values are agreed by IETF consensus, and the top fifteen are left for private use.

viz.caption: THE THREE LEVELS OF MBMS KEYS

root.label: MBMS User Key (MUK)
root.note: Point-to-point key between the multicast server and each client.

children.label: MBMS Service Key (MSK)
children.note: Group key between the multicast server and all the clients.

children.label: MBMS Traffic Key (MTK)
children.note: Group traffic key that protects the media traffic. The level that is updated often.

viz.caption: HOW MBMS HANDS THE KEYS DOWN

messages.label: MUK
messages.note: Shared point-to-point and used as the pre-shared key for MIKEY.

messages.label: MSK
messages.note: Delivered point-to-point under the MUK, and pushed to all clients as the second-level group key.

messages.label: MTK
messages.note: Pushed to all clients under the MSK as the third-level key that protects the media.

items.label: MBMS Key Domain ID
items.desc: ID of the group key domain.

items.label: MBMS Traffic Key ID
items.desc: ID of the group traffic key.

viz.caption: THE TWO SECURITY TRADE-OFFS OF BROADCAST KEY UPDATES

items.title: No source authentication on the traffic key
items.text: The traffic key is protected by a group MAC keyed by the service key, so group members can try to spoof updates. 3GPP judged the risk acceptable.

items.title: Not compatible with SRTP-TESLA
items.text: SRTP-TESLA requires source origin authentication of the integrity key, which this delivery method does not provide.

items.title: Policy delivered apart from the key
items.text: The security policy travels with the service key, because traffic key updates can be a few seconds apart and carrying the policy each time would be costly.
